The silhouette width [@rousseeuw1987silhouettes] measures, for each
observation, how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the nearest
other cluster. **Silhouette** computes silhouette widths from an
$n \times K$ matrix: the distances (or similarities) from each observation to
each of $K$ clusters, or the membership probabilities that soft and model-based
clustering methods return. It does not need the $n \times n$ matrix of
pairwise dissimilarities that the classical silhouette uses, so it works for
large data sets and for fuzzy and probabilistic clusterings.

The widths computed here are therefore not the classical widths of
`cluster::silhouette()`. They follow the simplified silhouette of
@vanderlaan2003pam and its extensions; the vignette
`vignette("interpreting-widths", package = "Silhouette")` explains how they
relate to the classical widths and how to read them.

```{r library}
library(Silhouette)
```

# Which function do I need?

| What you have | Function |
|:---|:---|
| Distances or similarities from each observation to each cluster (for example, to k-means centroids or PAM medoids) | `Silhouette()` |
| Membership or posterior probabilities (fuzzy c-means, Gaussian mixtures, probabilistic distance clustering) | `softSilhouette()`, `cerSilhouette()`, `dbSilhouette()` |
| Both, and you want every applicable width at once | `calSilhouette()` |
| Silhouette results for several modes of a block or multi-way clustering | `extSilhouette()` |
| Widths computed elsewhere that you want to summarize or plot | `getSilhouette()` |
| A silhouette object from **cluster**, **factoextra** or **drclust** | `plotSilhouette()` |

Every width function returns an object of class `"Silhouette"`: a data frame
with one row per observation (columns `cluster`, `neighbor`, `sil_width`, and
`weight` for fuzzy averaging) that has `summary()` and `plot()` methods.

# A first example: k-means

The k-means result contains the cluster centers but not the distances to them,
so we compute the $n \times K$ Euclidean distances with `proxy::dist()` and pass
them to `Silhouette()`.

```{r kmeans}
X <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4])
set.seed(1)
km <- kmeans(X, centers = 3, nstart = 20)
P <- proxy::dist(X, km$centers)   # 150 x 3 distances to the centers
sil <- Silhouette(P)
head(sil, 4)
```

Each observation is assigned to its nearest cluster (`cluster`) and compared
with the next nearest (`neighbor`). The width is
$(b_i - a_i)/\max(a_i, b_i)$, where $a_i$ and $b_i$ are the distances to those
two clusters, so it lies between 0 and 1: values near 1 mean the observation is
much closer to its own cluster, values near 0 mean it sits between two clusters.

```{r kmeans-summary}
s <- summary(sil, print.summary = FALSE)
s$avg.width      # average width over all observations
s$sil.sum        # size and average width of each cluster
```

```{r kmeans-plot, fig.alt = "Silhouette plot of 150 iris flowers in three k-means clusters. One cluster has widths mostly above 0.75; the other two have lower widths, several close to zero, with the average marked by a dashed line near 0.67."}
plot(sil)
```

The plot sorts the widths within each cluster and marks the overall average.
The cluster of *setosa* flowers is compact and well separated; the other two
clusters overlap, and a few of their observations have widths close to zero.

The argument `method = "pac"` uses the normalization of
@raymaekers2022silhouettes, $(b_i - a_i)/(a_i + b_i)$. It ranks the
observations in the same order as the default and gives smaller values: each
PAC width equals $s_i/(2 - s_i)$, where $s_i$ is the default width.

```{r pac}
sil_pac <- Silhouette(P, method = "pac")
all.equal(sil_pac$sil_width, sil$sil_width / (2 - sil$sil_width))
```

# Scoring a partition from elsewhere

A silhouette scores a partition. By default `Silhouette()` takes it from the
matrix, assigning each observation to its nearest cluster, which for k-means is
the partition the algorithm produced. For other methods, pass the partition as
`cluster` (column numbers of the matrix). Here an average-linkage partition is
scored against the centroids of its own groups:

```{r cluster-arg}
hc <- cutree(hclust(dist(X), method = "average"), k = 3)
centers <- apply(X, 2, function(v) tapply(v, hc, mean))
sil_hc <- Silhouette(proxy::dist(X, centers), cluster = hc)
summary(sil_hc, print.summary = FALSE)$avg.width
sum(sil_hc$sil_width < 0)   # flowers closer to another group's centroid
```

Observations that are closer to another cluster's centroid than to their own
receive negative widths. Without `cluster`, they would silently be moved to the
nearest centroid and a different partition would be scored. Memberships passed
as `prob_matrix` play the same role: each observation keeps the cluster with
its largest membership.

# Letting a clustering function do the work

Many clustering functions return the proximity matrix themselves. Instead of
extracting it, you can pass the function as `clust_fun`, its arguments through
`...`, and the name of the component to use. Here fuzzy c-means from
**ppclust** returns the distances in component `d` and the memberships in
component `u`:

```{r fcm-oneline}
set.seed(1)
sil_fcm <- Silhouette(prox_matrix = "d", prob_matrix = "u", average = "fuzzy",
                      clust_fun = ppclust::fcm, x = X, centers = 3)
summary(sil_fcm, print.summary = FALSE)$avg.width
```

With `average = "fuzzy"`, the average weights each observation by how decisively
it is assigned, following @campello2006fuzzy.

One caution: `ppclust::fcm()` stores **squared** Euclidean distances in `d`.
Squaring every distance changes each width from $s_i$ to $s_i(2 - s_i)$, which
is larger. To work on the Euclidean scale, fit the model first and take square
roots:

```{r fcm-sqrt}
set.seed(1)
fm <- ppclust::fcm(X, centers = 3)
summary(Silhouette(sqrt(fm$d), prob_matrix = fm$u, average = "fuzzy"),
        print.summary = FALSE)$avg.width
```

# Soft and model-based clustering

When all you have is a matrix of membership or posterior probabilities, use
`softSilhouette()`. For a Gaussian mixture fitted with **mclust**, the
posterior probabilities are in component `z`:

```{r mclust}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(mclust))  # Mclust() needs mclust attached
gm <- Mclust(X, G = 3, verbose = FALSE)
sil_gm <- softSilhouette(gm$z)
summary(sil_gm, print.summary = FALSE)$avg.width
```

`calSilhouette()` computes every width that its inputs allow and returns one
table, with crisp, membership-weighted (fuzzy) and median averages:

```{r calsil}
calSilhouette(prob_matrix = gm$z)
```

The rows are different indices on different scales, so compare each row across
fits, never the rows with each other. They are also not independent evidence:
several rows are monotone transformations of one another (see
`?calSilhouette`). The rows computed from memberships are the silhouettes of
@bhatkapu2024density (PACS, PPS, NLPPS, PDS and the certainty silhouette CeS)
and the density-based silhouette of @menardi2011density; to choose the number
of clusters they are read differently from the distance-based widths. The
vignette
`vignette("soft-clustering", package = "Silhouette")` explains each index and
when to use it.

# Choosing the number of clusters

A common use of the average width is to compare partitions with different
numbers of clusters and pick the one with the **largest** average.

```{r choose-k, fig.alt = "Line chart of the average simplified silhouette width for k-means on the iris data against the number of clusters from 2 to 6. The average is highest at 2 clusters and lower for every larger number."}
avg_width <- sapply(2:6, function(k) {
  set.seed(k)
  km <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 20)
  s <- Silhouette(proxy::dist(X, km$centers))
  summary(s, print.summary = FALSE)$avg.width
})
plot(2:6, avg_width, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of clusters", ylab = "Average silhouette width")
```

For the iris measurements the average is highest at two clusters, because
*versicolor* and *virginica* overlap; the silhouette favors compact,
well-separated groups rather than the three species. Choosing the number of
clusters needs more than one index, and the widths computed from posterior
probabilities behave differently again (see
`vignette("soft-clustering", package = "Silhouette")`).
